examples: *If the app* disrupts the market, *we will* double our team. (a real future result)
We *will* start the migration *as soon as* the servers are ready. (time clause stays in the present simple)
The old system *will* stay online *until* every client switches. (until = the limit)
*When* you find the bottleneck, *we will* fix it together. (when + present, will in the main clause)
*Before* you deprecate the feature, *warn* the users. (warning before an action)
*After* the gamification update ships, engagement *will* rise. (sequence of events)
grammar.explanation:
We use the **first conditional** to talk about real future possibilities. Its pattern is simple: **if + present simple, will + verb**.

**If we disrupt** the market with this launch, we **will** attract serious investors. The condition is realistic, not imaginary.

Future time clauses follow the same logic. After **when**, **until**, **as soon as**, **before**, and **after**, use the **present simple** — never **will**.

We **will** release the update **as soon as** the latency tests pass. The time clause stays in the present, even though it points to the future.

**Until** sets a limit. The team **won't** deprecate the old tool **until** every client migrates. Nothing happens before that moment.

Watch out for one classic trap: never put **will** inside the **if**-clause or the time clause. Say **if you have** the bandwidth, not **if you will have** the bandwidth.
